DeWitt Wallace, Epsilon 14, Founded, Edits and
Publishes World's Most Popular Magazine
It is a favorite theme of Brother DeWitt WaUace that
individual man, supported by faith and determination, can
make an imprint on society as clearly as a skier leaves his
tracks on driven snow.
The magazine he founded in 1922 stands as a great
testament to the efficacy of this belief. Launched amid
dire prophecies of failure by leading publishers with
whom he discussed his idea. The Reader's Digest has be
come the world's most successful and influential magazine.
The man who began this unique publishing enterprise
was bom on November 12, 1889 in St. Paul, Minnesota.
His father was Dr. James Wallace, who was successively
professor, dean and president of Macalester College, a lib
eral arts institution in St. Paul, Minnesota.
Brother Wallace entered Macalester College in 1907.
His interest in scholastic matters, never unduly high, had
waned sufficiently by the end of his sophomore year to
influence him to take a summer job in a bank in the state
of Colorado headed by his uncle, Robert Wallace. He
stayed a full year, during which he began to take more
seriously a pastime that had entertained him at Macales
ter: noting and filing highlights from magazine articles
that he considered of more than just passing interest and
value.
In 1910 DeWitt Wallace enrolled at the University of
California at Berkeley where he was initiated into Psi Up
silon. In 1912 he returned to St. Paul and took a job writ
ing sales promotion letters for the Book Department of
the Webb Publishing Company.
While he was with Webb, his magazine articles gathered
momentum and took on a somewhat different direction.
He noted that the U.S. Department of Agriculture and
various state agriculture departments had published liundreds of pamphlets on a wide variety of subjects. He
thought that these would be of great use to farmers, if
they could be made aware of their existence.
The result of this wish to help farmers help them
selves was "Getting the Most Out of Farming," a 124page booklet which listed titles of the free pamphlets to
gether with brief summaries of their contents. Brother
Wallace sold 100,000 copies of the booklet, largely to
banks for distribution to their farmer customers.
In the months that followed he honed his condensing
techniques, working next on a digest of ideas from market
ing trade journals that he hoped to sell to department
stores. While working on this booklet, he was struck by
the idea that condensation could work as well with articles
of general interest as with those of specific application.
America's entry in World War I in 1917 (temporarily)
ended DeWitt Wallace's growing preoccupation, but he
was soon to pick it up again. Seriously wounded in the
Meuse-Argonne offensive in 1918, he spent his four
months' convalescence reading and condensing general-in
terest magazine articles.
Discharged in 1919, he continued his work in the Min
neapolis Public Library. In 1920 he felt enough confidence
in what he was doing to issue a sample copy of what he
called The Reader's Digest. It contained the best of his
condensations. Wallace circulated it to publishers, and
offered his services as editor to anyone who would support
his idea and hire him to implement it.
The lack of interest was universal. Even such a bril
liantly instinctive publisher as William Randolph Hearst
prophesied a small circulation for such a magazine.
After all, how could a publication without fiction, adver
tising or artwork and with only serious articles possibly
attract more than few readers?
Yet he did have at least one staunch supporter. She
was Lila Bell Acheson, the sister of a Macalester College
classmate whom Wallace had met on a Christmas vacation
spent at the Achesons' Tacoma, Washington home.
Brother DeWitt Wallace, Epsilon '14,
and his wife, Lila, are co-founders and
co-chairmen of THE READER'S DI
GEST, the world's most popular mag
azine. Besides literary activity, the
Wallace's have distinguished them
selves by giving substantial support to
many diversified projects ranging
from Macalester College to the res
toration of the Villa Boscobel. Mrs.
Wallace's gift of $1 million accounted
for almost all of the money needed for
the new YWCA Center in White
Plains, New York. Brother Wallace is
also a member of the President's
Diamond Club.

When the publishers to whom he had shown his Read
er's Digest failed to respond, Wallace took a job in the
International Publicity Department of the Westinghouse
Electric Company in Pittsburgh.
At this time an associate, a mail-order specialist, con
vinced him that The Reader's Digest could (successfully)
be sold by mail. One day Brother Wallace's boss said, "As
I understand you are planning to start a magazine, and as
you were the last one hired, you will have to leave May
31." Others in the department were dismissed soon after
because of the depression.
With $5,000 of (mostly borrowed) capital. Brother
Wallace spent the next four months in Pittsburgh mail
ing letters offering a year's subscription to the yet-to-be
born magazine. Then on October 15, 1921, Wallace and
Lila Acheson were married at Pleasantville, New York.
Soon after returning from the honeymoon. The Reader's
Digest was launched with an initial circulation of about
1,500 copies.
Today, 45 years later, the magazine is published in 14
languages and 30 separate editions. Over 25 million copies
are bought each month.
Digest Headquarters
The Digest headquarters is a story in itself. Formerly
the central office operations of The Digest were concur
rently conducted from 14 different locations in the town
of Pleasantville. Most of the aforementioned operations are
now conducted from one location in Chappaqua, but the
frantic atmosphere usually associated with the publishing
business is strangely absent. The informality is astounding.
People calling DeWitt Wallace are startled to have him
answer his own phone. There are no regular meetings or
fixed editorial routines. This operation prompted writer
James Wood to say, "editorial communication (at Digest
headquarters) is by osmosis and contagion."
Writers who are invited to discuss articles and ideas
are entertained at a beautifully restored 180-year old farm
house. An invitation to have lunch in Chappaqua can be
the beginning of a bonanza for writer and reader alike.
A series of events recounted by John Reddy in the 1965
edition of Writer's Yearbook illustrated this point effec
tively.
A few years ago a free lance writer named Cornelius
Ryan had lunch with a group of editors at The Reader's
Digest to discuss new article possibilities. After hashing
over a number of ideas that elicited little enthusiasm from
the assembly. Digest Executive Editor Hobart Lewis asked
Ryan what he would like to write if he could write any
thing he wanted to.
Ryan replied that he had always wanted to write
something about D-Day because he felt that the first 24
hours of the invasion were the most fateful in recent his
tory. After a little discussion, all warmed to the subject
and when the lunch ended he had an assignment to do a
D-Day piece for The Digest.
When Ryan submitted the results of his first research
effort, the editors of The Digest were enthusiastic. They
decided the subject would make a good book. Simon
and Schuster and The Digest gave Ryan an advance which
enabled him to write the book; The Digest also assigned
its research departments in the United States and Europe
to assist Ryan.
The Longest Day, Ryan's book, was condensed in two
issues of The Digest. The Simon and Schuster hard-cover
edition sold over 80,000 copies and was on the non-fiction
best seller list for five months. The paperback edition sold
almost 1 and %, million copies. The motion picture of the
same name produced by Darryl Zanuck with a screen play
by Ryan, grossed more money than any black and white
picture in history.

A University's Reputation
There are more than 2,000 institutions in the United
States that call themselves coUege or university. Some of
them rank among the greatest centers of higher learning
in the world; others do not bear comparison with good
high schools. Some cost a great deal to attend, others (in
cluding some of the best) almost nothing. Some are
church-afiiliated, some are secular. Some offer only the
liberal arts; others are essentially trade schools.
With such numbers and diversity, it is not enough to
conclude that there is some place for almost everybody
who wants to go to college. The fact is that there are
several some places for almost everybody. The interest
ing question then becomes: why does this student go to
that college?
There are a few obvious determinants�
academic apti
tude and achievement, ability to pay, geography�
but they
are not exclusive. Even students of low ability have a fair
number of choices among public and private institutions;
those of average or high ability have an even larger choice.
The same is true of cost. There are a lot of inexpensive
schools and a lot of expensive ones, and even within one
school there are students from families with wide varia
tion in income. As for geography, most Americans do tend
to go to a college in their own state and, within the state,
to an institution in the area where they live. But the lines
of demarcation are not neat. While a public urban insti
tution may draw its students almost exclusively from the
city in which it is located, the pool of potential recruits
for a
religious college is composed primarily of communi
cants of that faith. And some colleges have a national
clientele.
It is, in short, a buyer's market in education. While col
leges do choose their students, to a much greater extent
students are in a position to choose their colleges. This
results in the process social scientists call self-selection,
and a central thread through the whole complex of that
process, a group at the University of California believes,
is that intangible but potent force, institutional image.
(We generally try to avoid using that word the way ad
vertising men and sociologists do, but we are going to in
this instance because no other word quite fills the bill.

gon State '48.
Presumably that is why advertising men and sociologists
use it too.) Prospective students perceive a school not
only in terms of its formal requirements but as a "kind"
of place�
although, as we shall see, some institutions do
not have strong images of any sort.
Like prophecies, college images can be self-fulfilling.
They have powerful reach and pulling power, drawing
some kinds of students and repelling others. A bright
and serious student may be attracted by a place with a
name for serious scholarship; by attending it he helps
validate that reputation. Another bright but not so seri
ous student may choose an easy college near good ski
ing country, and he and his leisure-minded fellows like
wise help fulfill that school's image.
The negative pull operates very strongly too, which is
one reason why it is so difficult to reverse, or even arrest,
the downward spiral of an institution that is already on
the skids. If a school has a widening reputation for medi
ocrity, what is important is not so much that mediocre
students will seek it as that good students will shun it.
All of this may seem very obvious, but like many ob
vious propositions it is accompanied by a host of subtle
ties. Colleges have reputations for other things than aca
demic standing, and they are part of the composite image.
Furthermore, understanding the power of institutional
reach helps explain the extraordinary variation in the char
acteristics of the student bodies found in different insti
tutions.
Several years ago, the Center for the Study of Higher
Education of the University of California at Berkeley, with
support of a Carnegie grant, embarked on an intensive
study of eight colleges to try to assess the kinds of im
pact different kinds of institutions have on their students
during their college careers. How do students change, if
at all, in attitudes, values, and aspirations? Do they change
more in one kind of institution than in another? In what
ways?
The study involves measures of the students from the
time they entered college until they left (and in some
cases after), analyses of the different institutions, and the
effect of institution on student.
We are not going to scoop the findings of the "change"
portion of the study, which will be fully reported in a
book to be published in a year or so. What we are dis-
